title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Miami, FL: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Miami welders and inspectors: hurricane-code steel, aluminum D1.2, bridges, and where to sit Parts A, B and C. Request a quote.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Miami: A Six-Day Course for South Florida Welders and Inspectors
html:
Miami has an unusual link to welding inspection. The American Welding Society, the body that administers the Certified Welding Inspector examination and issues the certification, lists its national headquarters address in Miami, and the city appears on the AWS list of seminar and examination sites. The six-day (6-day) course Atlantis NDT runs for South Florida readies welders, fitters, QC inspectors, NDT technicians and engineers in Miami-Dade for the AWS CWI examination. Work through it online whenever your hours allow, or have your employer bring the six days to its own premises for several staff at once. Atlantis has no Miami classroom and certifies no one: it prepares candidates for an examination that AWS writes, runs and scores. To scope it for yourself or a crew, request a Miami CWI prep quote.

Why welding inspection demand concentrates in South Florida

Miami-Dade builds tall, builds near salt water and builds under a hurricane code. Those three facts shape almost every welding inspection job in the county. A structural steel connection on a tower in Brickell, an aluminum guardrail on a condominium balcony, a gangway at a cruise terminal and a bascule bridge leaf over the Miami River are all welded, and each one sits under a different set of acceptance rules. Contractors, testing laboratories, fabricators and public agencies need people who can read those rules, measure what was built and say yes or no with a signature that holds up.

The workforce here is also distinctive. Many experienced Miami welders learned the trade on jobsites in Latin America and the Caribbean, often with years of hands-on work and little formal schooling. The AWS eligibility rules were written for exactly that kind of career: they trade education against years of welding-related experience, so a welder with a long work record can qualify without a degree. What such a candidate usually lacks is not skill but exam vocabulary, symbol reading and practice finding answers inside a code book under time pressure. That gap is what a structured six-day preparation is for.

Hurricane-code buildings and the inspection chain behind them

Miami-Dade and Broward are the two counties the Florida Building Code places in its High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, which carries tougher wind-load provisions than the rest of the state. Steel framing, moment connections, embedded plates, stair stringers, canopy frames and curtain-wall supports all have to resist those loads, and many of them are joined by field welds made at height in wind and rain. The welds that carry the load are typically specified to AWS D1.1, the structural steel welding code that the steel design standards point to.

Florida law adds a layer for larger buildings. Structures the statute classes as threshold buildings, generally the taller ones and large assembly occupancies, must have a special inspector, who is a licensed engineer or architect certified for that role. The special inspector cannot stand under every weld, so the hands-on checking of structural welding is commonly done by welding inspectors employed by testing laboratories or by the steel erector's quality program, and the CWI credential is the usual way those inspectors show they are qualified. Building departments and engineers of record in the county read inspection reports from CWIs every week.

What does that inspector actually do on a Miami high-rise? Checks the welder's qualification records against the work, confirms the procedure being used fits the joint, watches fit-up and preheat on thick connections, measures fillet sizes and groove reinforcement after welding, and writes down every reject with a location the erector can find. Every one of those tasks appears somewhere in the three parts of the CWI examination, which is why the exam suits people already doing the job informally.

Aluminum, stainless steel and salt air

Walk any Miami Beach or Brickell building and you will find more welded aluminum than in most American cities: balcony and stair railings, pool fences, sunshades, canopy frames, marina gangways and boat-lift structures. Structural aluminum welding is governed by AWS D1.2, Structural Welding Code, Aluminum, and AWS offers D1.2 as one of its Part C code books (the 2014 edition at the time of writing). For an inspector at an aluminum railing or storefront fabricator, choosing D1.2 for Part C means studying the book they will actually work from.

Aluminum behaves differently from steel, and the exam expects inspectors to know why. It shows no temper colors as it heats, so a welder gets less visual warning. Hydrogen from moisture, oil or the oxide layer causes porosity, which makes cleaning and filler wire storage inspection points rather than housekeeping. Heat-treated alloys lose strength next to the weld, which the design side of D1.2 accounts for and the inspector has to respect by making sure the joint matches the drawing. Stainless steel, common on marine hardware and coastal architecture, brings its own checks: heat tint, contamination from carbon steel tools, and the corrosion that follows when either is ignored near salt spray.

The waterfront: cruise terminals, river yards and marinas

PortMiami is one of the busiest cruise ports anywhere, and building and maintaining its terminals, passenger boarding bridges, gangways, mooring hardware and cargo cranes generates steady welding and inspection work. Up the Miami River, small shipyards and terminals serve the coastal freighters and tugs that trade with the Caribbean, and the wider South Florida coast supports a large yacht repair and refit sector. Marine work mixes codes: shore structures usually fall under the structural codes, while welding on classed vessels is accepted by the classification society's surveyor under its own rules, with a CWI often acting as the yard's or owner's quality inspector rather than the final authority.

Inspectors in marine work tend to meet corrosion, distortion and repair welding more than new construction, so the fundamentals material on discontinuities, metallurgy and nondestructive testing matters a great deal. If your work also involves thickness gauging or crack detection on marine steel, see ultrasonic testing in marine work and visual testing in Miami for how the NDT side fits alongside the CWI role.

Bascule bridges, causeways and FDOT District Six

The Miami River is crossed by a string of bascule (draw) bridges, and the causeways to the barrier islands add more moveable spans and long steel and concrete structures. The Florida Department of Transportation's District Six, which covers Miami-Dade and Monroe counties, manages a large inventory of these structures, along with the signal mast arms and overhead sign structures that line the county's roads. Mast arms and sign trusses are welded tubular steel, and their welds are inspected in the fabricator's shop before they ever reach the street.

Steel bridge members are welded under AWS D1.5, Bridge Welding Code, which AWS offers as a Part C book (the 2020 edition, including its clause on fracture-critical members). A candidate who works for a bridge fabricator, a bascule repair contractor or a consultant inspecting for the department should look hard at D1.5 rather than defaulting to D1.1. For background on how inspectors approach these structures, read bridge and structural steel inspection and the summary of the AWS D1.5 bridge welding code.

Sitting the AWS exam from Miami

Each of the three CWI exam parts is scored on its own, and AWS sets the bar at 72 percent for every one of them. Part A, Fundamentals, has 150 questions and is a computer-based test. Part B, Practical, is 46 questions tied to hands-on activities with equipment AWS provides. Part C, Code Book, is open book, runs from 50 to 65 questions depending on the code, and is also computer-based.

Where you take each part matters for planning:

  • Part B is given only at AWS seminar locations, on fixed dates. Miami is on the AWS list of seminar and exam sites as of November 2026, so a South Florida candidate can often sit the practical without travel. Check aws.org for the dates actually scheduled; the list and calendar change.
  • Parts A and C are delivered by Prometric at proctored test centers, not at home or at work. You schedule them after AWS sends a confirmation letter with an eligibility code.
  • Deadlines: for US Part B dates, AWS sets the application deadline roughly six weeks before the exam. Count back from the date you want and leave margin for gathering experience letters.

If the Miami dates do not suit you, Tampa is the other Florida site on the AWS list; see CWI exam prep in Tampa. The national page on the six-day AWS CWI exam prep course explains each part in more depth, and this breakdown of Parts A, B and C covers where candidates tend to struggle.

Welding schools and the AWS South Florida Section

Most CWIs start as welders, and Miami-Dade County Public Schools runs technical colleges that teach the trade. Robert Morgan Educational Center and Technical College and Miami Lakes Educational Center and Technical College both list welding technology programs. Formal trade or vocational coursework of that kind counts on the AWS eligibility table, where it lowers the years of experience required compared with a high school diploma alone, so keep your transcripts.

The AWS South Florida Section, part of AWS District 5, is the local chapter for the Miami area. Section meetings and plant tours are a practical way to meet working inspectors, hear which code books local employers use, and find other candidates preparing for the same exam date. Joining is optional and separate from certification, but the contacts help when you need someone to confirm your work experience on an application.

How the six days fit a Miami candidate or employer

The course follows the same six-block outline in every format. Days one and two cover fundamentals: welding processes, AWS terminology, joint design and welding symbols, then metallurgy, testing, discontinuities, safety and the inspector's duties. Day three is practical preparation for Part B: gauges, weld size and profile, and applying acceptance criteria and procedure records. Day four is working inside the code book you chose for Part C. Day five is timed practice papers for all three parts, and day six goes back over weak areas and exam-day logistics.

For an individual, that outline becomes an online study plan with materials, original practice questions and instructor support by message when a topic does not click. Many Miami candidates work long days on jobsites and in the summer storm season, so working at your own pace is often the only realistic way to prepare. The practice questions are written to the published body of knowledge; none is taken from a real AWS examination.

For a contractor, laboratory or fabricator that wants several people ready at once, the six days can be delivered at your own facility. That lets the practical day use your gauges and your weld samples, whether those are moment-connection mockups, aluminum railing joints or repair coupons from a marine job, so the practice matches what your inspectors accept every week. Atlantis's offices are in Houston and Hyderabad; for an on-site course we send the instructor to you.

Choosing a Part C code book for Miami work

Part C lets you nominate a code, so pick the one matching the jobs on your desk today or the ones you are chasing next year. These are the books from the AWS list most relevant to Miami employers:

Typical Miami workCode book to considerWhy
High-rise and commercial structural steel, stairs, canopiesAWS D1.1 (2020)The structural steel welding code most building work is specified to
Aluminum railings, storefronts, gangways, sunshadesAWS D1.2 (2014)Covers structural aluminum, common in coastal construction
Steel bridge members, bascule leaf repairsAWS D1.5 (2020)Required for highway bridge steel, including fracture-critical members
Power plant pipingASME B31.1 (2024)Power piping code used at generating stations
Process piping in industrial plantsASME B31.3 (2024)Process piping code; see the B31.3 summary

Still torn? Structural candidates lean toward D1.1 more than any other book. To see what studying it involves, browse our summary of the structural steel code, then read how its visual acceptance limits are applied on real joints.

Eligibility, the vision test and the paperwork

AWS decides who may sit the examination. Its eligibility table pairs schooling with years of welding-related work. A welding engineering or welding technology bachelor's needs a single year; a relevant associate degree, two; a high school diploma, five; eighth-grade schooling, nine; anything less, twelve. Every candidate must also pass a vision test. Those requirements are the candidate's to meet; the course does not change them.

AWS asks for experience that an employer or supervisor can confirm. If some of your years were with employers outside the United States, line up people who can confirm that work before you apply, and ask AWS directly if you are unsure whether a job qualifies. A new CWI's certification lasts nine years in total; AWS wants a renewal application at year three and again at year six, then recertification when year nine arrives. For a full picture of the requirements, read CWI requirements and career impact.

Request a quote for Miami CWI exam prep

Tell us whether you are an individual or an employer, how many people need preparation, which code book each person plans to choose for Part C, and roughly when you hope to sit the exam. Employers should also say where the course would be held and what weld samples and gauges are available on site. We reply within one business day. Current AWS examination and seminar fees are posted on aws.org; to plan the full budget, see the CWI exam fee planning guide. When you are ready, send a Miami CWI prep enquiry.

Some Miami inspectors pair the CWI with nondestructive testing qualifications so they can perform the tests a welding inspector otherwise has to request. Atlantis trains to ASNT SNT-TC-1A for that side of the work, under which your employer certifies you; see NDT training in Miami and VT Level 2 training. Florida candidates further north can read about CWI exam prep in Jacksonville, and Georgia candidates near the AWS site in Kennesaw can see CWI exam prep in Atlanta.

faq.q: Can I take the CWI practical exam in Miami?
faq.a: Miami is on the AWS list of seminar and examination sites as of November 2026, and Part B is only given at those sites on fixed dates. Check aws.org for the dates actually scheduled before you plan around them.

faq.q: Where do Miami candidates take Parts A and C?
faq.a: Parts A and C are computer-based tests delivered by Prometric at proctored test centers. You book them after AWS sends a confirmation letter with an eligibility code; they cannot be taken at home.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a classroom in Miami?
faq.a: No. Atlantis's offices are in Houston and Hyderabad. Miami candidates study online, or an employer can have the six-day course delivered at its own facility.

faq.q: Which Part C code book suits high-rise steel work in Miami?
faq.a: Most structural steel candidates choose AWS D1.1. If your work is mainly bridge steel, D1.5 is the better fit, and aluminum fabricators should look at D1.2. See the national course page for the full list AWS offers.

faq.q: Is AWS D1.2 a sensible choice for aluminum railing and canopy fabricators?
faq.a: Yes, if aluminum is what you inspect. AWS offers D1.2, the structural aluminum code, as a Part C option, so you can prepare with the book you use at work.

faq.q: Can my Miami company have the six days run at our shop or yard?
faq.a: Yes. An employer can have the six-day course delivered at its own facility for a group of staff, and the practical day can use the company's own gauges and weld samples. Request a quote.

faq.q: Does finishing the course make me a Certified Welding Inspector?
faq.a: No. That credential comes only from AWS, which runs the exam and grants the certification once you clear it. Six days of study get you ready; eligibility, the vision test and all three parts remain yours to meet.

faq.q: How much experience does a welder with a high school diploma need?
faq.a: The AWS table asks for five years of welding-related experience with a high school diploma or equivalent. Other education levels shift that number up or down; check the current table on aws.org.

faq.q: Can I list welding experience I gained outside the United States?
faq.a: AWS asks for experience an employer or supervisor can confirm. If your work was abroad, arrange contacts who can verify it before you apply, and ask AWS if you are unsure the work qualifies.

faq.q: How does a CWI fit into threshold building inspection in Florida?
faq.a: Threshold buildings require a special inspector who is a licensed engineer or architect. Hands-on structural weld checks on those projects are commonly done by CWIs working for testing laboratories or the steel contractor's quality program.
